prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes aggregate productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection is the contribution I can defend most cleanly on the common criteria of originality, influence, attribution and maturity. Melitz (2003) is a precisely identifiable core model. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI and through his broader role in trade theory, supplies a defensible second name. The framework moved trade from representative industries to firm-level microdata, and it explains who exports, why gains from trade are reallocative, and how trade affects aggregate productivity. It is now standard in trade, macro and industrial organisation. After more than twenty years it has been replicated and extended across many countries and datasets. The attribution fits a two-person award with little arbitrary cutting, which is not true of B014 (eight credited names), B032 (Dorn/Katz) or B044 (seven names). Krugman's 2008 prize covered earlier new trade theory and did not cover this strand. Reconsidering after reading colleagues, I keep B010 first because its credit line is cleaner than the other broadly supported candidates, not because of any count of first-place votes. B010 also has relatively wide support: ten of eleven members ranked it and its credited pair is nearly identical across proposals.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributed closely related empirical and theoretical work, and those names are not credited on this ballot, so a Helpman-Melitz award could look like a partial cut through a larger lineage. The quantitative welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. Some quantitative work suggests the selection-based gains are smaller than first claimed. Finally, trade is not my field. I rely on the common criteria and on colleagues' accounts of the trade literature, and I cannot independently confirm the priority questions.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B010 second but notes that Helpman appears across several trade candidates, which could split support. He also notes that quantitative work suggests the welfare gains from selection may be smaller than first claimed, and that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum could be seen as co-originators.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap with B003 and B041 is a real practical risk. But I treat it as a reason to keep the credit narrow, to Melitz and Helpman, and not as a reason against the contribution. I would separate the framework from the size of the gains. The framework explains exporter selection and within-industry reallocation, and that robust firm-level evidence does not depend on the magnitude of the welfare gains. Those gains are debated, and the debate is conducted in the framework's own language, which I read as a sign of influence. I accept that the citation should not claim a specific welfare magnitude. It should rest on the mechanism, which is why I word it around reallocation and selection.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B032 first. She argues that it joins a conceptual framework (tasks, building on skill-biased change) with credible quasi-experimental evidence. She also concedes that a three-person cap forces the omission of Dorn, a core China-shock co-author, so the attribution split is a real judgement call.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case for B032, and I ranked it fourth among the candidates I examined, partly because of the design-based credibility of the evidence. My difference is about attribution, which is where the concern she raises bites. Two strands, tasks and skill premium (Autor, Katz) and the China shock (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), are being combined under a three-name cap. Whichever of Dorn or Katz is dropped leaves a real contributor out. I would also want the committee to decide whether it is honouring one strand or both before it decides on names. That is why I keep B032 as a serious alternative and not my preferred part. If the committee chooses it, I would lean toward Autor and Hanson with either Katz or Dorn, depending on which strand the citation names, and I do not think the question can be settled by vote counts.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first with Melitz and Helpman. She treats Melitz (2003) as central and Helpman as a strong second credit. She leaves Redding off as later and more separable. She also flags the Melitz-Chaney and Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum antecedents that are not credited on this list.
responses.response: I largely agree, including on leaving Redding out of the core credit. His quantitative and spatial work looks like a separable later contribution. I would qualify one point. Because the Bernard et al. empirical facts are uncredited, the citation should be about the theoretical framework of firm heterogeneity and selection and its implications for gains from trade. It should not claim to have discovered exporter premia or firm-level stylised facts as such. That wording is accurate to the credited names and avoids implying that the empirical lineage belongs to them alone.

uncertainties: How the committee would treat the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum and with the quantitative Ricardian strand (B003), given that those names are not credited with Helpman and Melitz on this ballot.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work should be a third credited name or is better seen as a separate, later contribution.
How much weight the committee should place on the debate over the size of the selection-based welfare gains, which depend on functional-form assumptions.
Whether, on attribution grounds, B032 should be preferred over B010 if the committee can agree which strand (tasks or the China shock) it wants to honour.
I cannot independently verify priority and attribution details in the trade literature beyond my own knowledge and colleagues' stated views.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The documented connections are Uppsala and IFAU labour-economics co-authors and an institutional overlap at Stockholm University with the IIES macro group, which is not a co-authorship. None of the B010 credited names (Helpman, Melitz, Redding) appears in the profile as a co-author or close collaborator.
